items.title: Pay attention everyone. This is not a joke.
items.summary:
Pay attention everyone. This is not a joke.

This is an existential crisis for software. Most of the Mag7 is inside it.

Today showed what it looks like. Anthropic launched Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Meetings, and Microsoft dropped as much as 3%. Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot apps now open inside Claude. OpenAI gave businesses their own agents inside ChatGPT.

Software was a moat for 30 years because code was hard to write. Now code is the cheap part. My take: an office suite is a weekend project for any lab with enough compute. Anything you can describe in words, AI can now build.

So where does the moat go? Down the stack, to whatever you can't prompt into existence.

First stop is compute. The best models can't run without it, and Anthropic's own S-1 shows who it depends on: at least $121.3B with Google, $110B with Amazon, $44.9B with Microsoft and up to $120.5B with SpaceXAI. The company disrupting everyone's software is a tenant. Microsoft is both its landlord and today's victim.

After compute comes power, land, chips and launch. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent $201.9B in one quarter on buildings and equipment. They are not spending that on code.

My take: that splits the Mag7 in two. Amazon and Microsoft carry the most software risk. Meta has users and distribution, which no lab can copy in a weekend.

Apple is the interesting case. I don't think it gets disrupted, because Apple is a hardware company at heart: devices, chips, a supply chain nobody else has. But it has the devices and not the compute. My guess: that is why Apple should work with SpaceX. Both are hardware companies, just different kinds, so they complement each other instead of competing. If Apple doesn't plug into someone who owns compute, the AI labs come for its software layer next.

SpaceX is different. It launches its own rockets, 35 in one quarter. It has 11,100 satellites in orbit, its own spectrum, its own power and 13 GW of compute targeted by the end of 2027. You can clone an app in a weekend. You can't clone a launch pad. My guess: even a decade of head start would not close that gap.

It still takes part in the software shift, from the safe side. Grok Bot is a harness. Elon said it himself: "Going forward, @SpaceX will use the best back end model for any given task, including Claude Opus 5.5, MidJourney, Suno and other leading APIs." Models are swappable, so no model owns the user for long. Grok 5 is its own shot at the top.

In 2027 compute starts moving to orbit. Elon's own guess for the first StarMind computers is Q3 2027. No permit fight, no grid queue.

Software got cheap. Atoms did not. Whoever scales compute fastest decides which labs live, and the company that owns the atoms under all of it does not have to pick a winner.

$SPCX

items.title: There are rumors that OpenAI will release new frontier models this Friday, November 6, with a significant improvement ov
items.summary:
There are rumors that OpenAI will release new frontier models this Friday, November 6, with a significant improvement over GPT-6 Astra. One interesting claim is that the internal model was trained through games and intensive interactive environments, and that the next Sol may share the same training approach.

I went through several recent OpenAI research publications to understand what might be happening behind the scenes. While the rumored training details remain unconfirmed, there are some interesting clues.

1. The performance gap

On November 3, OpenAI published results from BenchCAD 2.0, evaluating AI models on mechanical design, 3D assemblies, and PCB connectivity.

GPT-6 Astra (Max): 0.594
New internal model: 0.875

That's a 28.1 percentage-point improvement on the benchmark.

We don't know how much of this comes from model architecture, additional training, or inference-time computation. But OpenAI has already confirmed that an earlier internal research model was developed through large-scale reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained model.

2. What caught my attention: training environments

In October, OpenAI published its collaboration with Ironclad, where researchers created executable software environments for AI agents to practice real professional workflows.

Instead of simply asking a model how to configure an approval process, they let the agent interact with the actual software, execute tasks, and evaluate the results against detailed criteria.

That changes the training process.

Traditional supervised training largely teaches a model to predict desired outputs. Interactive reinforcement learning allows it to experience the consequences of its actions and improve through feedback.

Observe → Act → Evaluate → Reward → Learn

Imagine applying the same idea to engineering.

An agent generates a CAD design, runs a simulation, discovers a mechanical conflict, adjusts the geometry, and tries again. Each attempt provides measurable feedback, rather than relying on whether the answer sounds correct.

This is a hypothetical example, not a confirmed description of OpenAI's internal training setup.

And the concept itself isn't new. We have seen reinforcement learning and self-play in systems such as AlphaGo and OpenAI Five.

What's interesting now is the possibility of scaling this approach across many different professional environments, with increasingly complex tasks and automated verification.

Related research such as SPADE also explores adaptive synthetic environments, where the difficulty of training tasks increases as the model improves.

3. Why the next Sol interests me

Another rumor suggests the upcoming Sol won't simply be distilled from the internal model, but will receive similar environment-based training.

If true, this could have important implications for smaller, cheaper models.

Distillation transfers knowledge from a stronger teacher. Direct reinforcement learning also allows a smaller model to develop its own behavior through interaction and feedback. The two methods can complement each other.

The question is whether a smaller model can gain substantial capability from better training environments without requiring the inference cost of the flagship model.

There is also an important distinction between model capability and the system running it. OpenAI's September mathematical research involved thousands of coordinated agents and enormous inference resources. Those results cannot be attributed to model training alone.

For me, the interesting direction here is how AI training may evolve from learning mostly through existing data and curated feedback toward practicing increasingly complex tasks in executable environments.

I'm especially interested in whether these improvements translate into better planning, error recovery, and reliable execution in unfamiliar situations.

4. Bringing this back to our own work

Our team is currently researching evaluation harnesses and trajectory judges for our own agents, looking beyond the final answer to evaluate the entire sequence of decisions, tool calls, and results.

One challenge I keep thinking about is that every major model improvement forces us to reconsider how the harness should work.

As models become more capable, we should be able to loosen the belt on how much freedom they have to reason, plan, and execute tasks, while keeping the critical boundaries controlled by the harness: what data can enter, what information can leave, and what actions the agent is authorized to perform.

The goal is to give better models more room to work, without giving them unrestricted access to the system.

That's what I think will make the next generation of agents particularly interesting: not only how much more capable the models become, but how we adapt our engineering around them.

items.title: Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.
items.summary:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

items.title: The AI Race is Putting Patients at Risk - Progressive.org
items.summary: Indeed, the most frightening risks involving AI are already moving from theory to capability. Frontier models let non-experts code new applications quickly, and soon it may be possible to use AI to create biological agents that can be weaponized. The White House’s own AI Action Plan warns that AI could create new pathways for bad actors to synthesize dangerous pathogens and calls for stronger screening and national security assessment of AI tools and systems. Anthropic has already said its [...] AI in health care offers many cases that regulatory frameworks should be addressing. A hospital can use AI for patient care and clinical decision support; an insurer for utilization management (e.g., automating care denials); a teenager for mental health advice; a public health department for outbreak detection; and a bad actor for infiltrating a hospital network. Different uses carry different risks and require separate risk-benefit analysis for determining regulatory guardrails. [...] Japan created an AI Strategy Headquarters headed by the prime minister and adopted a national AI basic plan. The United Kingdom and Australia are linking their AI safety institutes in order to better evaluate frontier AI model risks. These systems differ, but they have one thing in common - national AI governance.

items.title: AI Has Entered the Boardroom. Who’s Overseeing It? | Stanford Graduate School of Business
items.summary:
In the survey, 75% of directors said they used AI for research and market analysis, 55% for board prep and material summarization. Other common uses included strategic question generation and competitive benchmarking. Matthys says that board members would ideally like to use AI “to track and summarize board packages and more quickly understand year-to-year trends by using LLM tools rather than reading 80- to 100-page reports.” [...] The sooner the better, the researchers suggest. “Moving too slowly with AI governance means you may miss out on opportunities,” Saripalli says. “The board has fiduciary responsibility for anything that has impact at the product or service level.”

“The risk of not moving is as serious as the risk of AI systems running amok,” Matthys adds, noting how past technological shifts have left unprepared companies behind. “If you don’t keep up, there’s a risk that 20 years from now you won’t exist.” [...] ## In Brief

 A new survey finds that corporate boards are not keeping up with AI governance.
 Directors report that they are discussing and using AI, yet their boards lack a systematic approach to oversight.
 Companies that wait to define AI strategy and audit their AI use risk being left behind.

“We’re trying to change the wheels on the bus while driving it at 100 miles an hour downhill.”

items.title: Chapman Advances Healthcare AI Research and Training | Chapman Newsroom
items.summary:
Totonchy sees the skepticism around AI in higher education as an opportunity.  

“Generative AI quickly gained a negative reputation because it was seen as a tool for cheating,” she said. “That misses the point. These tools can work alongside humans, handling routine tasks so people can focus on analysis and decision-making. The sooner institutions move past resistance, the sooner AI can support that work.” 

STUDENTS PUT AI TO WORK [...] To address bias in clinical decision-making tools, Wang founded the Healthcare AI Initiative (HAI) at Chapman, bringing together researchers working on pressing healthcare challenges. HAI examines ethical questions surrounding AI, including data privacy, and develops equitable machine learning approaches.  

Wang also developed an AI elective within the School of Pharmacy, focused on practical applications for future clinicians. [...] “Every pharmacist has heard the rumors that AI will take pharmacists’ jobs,” Wang said. “But early exposure helps students. As future clinicians, they learn where the real focus should be in relation to AI. That’s something my students learn in this course.”  

Wang also works with students on research projects, extending that learning beyond the classroom. Two PharmD students, Elena Wu ’27 and Harvey Duong ’27, have collaborated with her on studies using AI to analyze large datasets.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5: Accelerating Physical Intelligence — Google DeepMind
items.summary:
Dexterity: Our robots can perform significantly more tasks with greater performance and dexterity — from using everyday tools to handling delicate, flexible objects.
 Reliability: During a real-world proof-of-concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines, our models helped Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid pick and pack automotive parts with a 96% success rate. This could enable robots to take on monotonous work, to enable technicians to focus on complex build tasks. [...] Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think, reason over multiple steps, and take action adapting to changes. In this proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 autonomously performs automotive kitting: the repetitive, physically taxing task of sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the exact order needed for each vehicle on the line. Offloading this monotonous prep work helps keep the assembly line moving, [...] With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.

items.title: Industrial automation startup Path Robotics raises $300M in funding - SiliconANGLE
items.summary: Path Robotics originally developed Obsidian for large robotic workstations called welding cells. In April, it introduced a four-legged robot called Rove that uses the model to automate shipbuilding tasks. The company says that its software can also be used to make parts for vehicles, power generators, utility poles and other heavy equipment. [...] Path Robotics has developed an AI model that addresses those challenges. Obsidian, as it’s called, is specifically designed to power industrial robots equipped with welding torches. The company says that the model can observe how metal parts change shape during the welding process and adjust its workflow accordingly. Furthermore, it automatically accounts for unexpected part variations. [...] Obsidian monitors the welding workflow using four lasers attached to the torch that it controls. The emitters illuminate the parts being welded together and the reflected light is captured by a pair of cameras. According to Path Robotics, Obsidian collects data not only during the welding process but also before and after each run.

Image 3: Daybreak for Critical Infrastructure — cover

Daybreak for Frontline Defenders Security Sep 3, 2026 [...] Share

OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem. [...] The agreement also builds on OpenAI’s existing work with cyber defenders in Poland. In July, CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, gained access⁠(opens in a new window) to OpenAI’s cyber capable models through Daybreak. The team used OpenAI models to help discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, including flaws that could be combined to take control of affected devices without authentication. The vendor released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed.

As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint. We also raised our bug bounty rewards to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed. Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through Daybreak Red.
